# Why CNNs Work for Images


## Image Properties

::: {#fig-cnn-example-rgb-image}
![[Image Source](https://unsplash.com/de/fotos/braune-schafe-auf-grunem-grasfeld-tagsuber-olonUwUrmQk)]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_small.png){width=70%}
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **High-dimensional** — $224 \times 224 \times 3 = 150{,}528$ values
- **Locality** — nearby pixels are correlated
- **Stability under transformations** — translations, color, rotations
- **Hierarchical structure** — pixels → edges → textures → objects
:::


## How are Nearby Pixels Related?

::: {.fragment}
- **Object coherence** — pixels in an object share color/texture
- **Smooth transitions** — gradual, not random
- **Texture patterns** — repeating local statistics
- **Edges/boundaries** — span multiple neighbors
:::


## MLPs Need Flat Inputs

::: {#fig-cnn-mlp}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}mlp_images_example.png){width=60%}

Image $\in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$ → flatten → vector $\in \mathbb{R}^p$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Flattening **destroys spatial structure**.
:::


## MLPs Explode in Size

::: {#fig-cnn-mlp-images}
![Source: @johnson_eecs_2019]({{< meta params.images_path >}}mlp_images.jpg){width=60%}
:::

::: {.fragment}
CIFAR-10 ($3 \times 32 \times 32$): a single first-layer neuron has **3,072 weights**.
:::


## What Does a Neuron Learn?

::: {#fig-cnn-mlp-example-weights}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}mlp_images_example_weights.png){width=60%}

A neuron's weights reshaped to image dimensionality reveal the pattern it detects.
:::


## MLPs Don't Generalize Across Positions

::: {#fig-cnns-mlp-pattern-shift}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}mlp_images_example_pattern_shifts.png){width=60%}

Same pattern, different positions — different weights light up.
:::


## Patterns at Different Locations

If an MLP learns "cat in the center", what about "cat in the corner"?

::: {.fragment}
- **Parameter explosion** — separate weights per position
- **Data hungry** — must see the pattern at every location
- **Poor generalization** — fails on unseen positions
:::

::: {.fragment}
[MLP Demo](https://adamharley.com/nn_vis/mlp/2d.html) — try drawing a digit at different positions.
:::


## MLPs on Images — Three Limitations {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- **High-dimensional** — size scales with input
- **No locality** — ignores spatial structure
- **No translation stability** — must learn position-specific patterns
:::


## Invariance and Equivariance

::: {.fragment}
**Invariant** — output unchanged by transformation:
$$f(g(\vect{x})) = f(\vect{x})$$
*"I don't care about the transformation."*
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Equivariant** — output transforms with input:
$$f(g(\vect{x})) = g(f(\vect{x}))$$
*"I transform my output the same way."*
:::


## Invariance — Classification

::: {#fig-cnns-invariance-example layout-ncol=2}

![Original]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_invariance_original.png)

![Translated]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_invariance_translate.png)

![Color-jittered]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_invariance_color.png)

![Rotated]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_invariance_rotate.png)

A classifier should produce **"cow"** in all four cases.
:::


## Equivariance — Detection

::: {#fig-cnns-equivariance-example layout-ncol=2}

![Original]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_equivariance_original.png)

![Shifted right]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_equivariance_shift_right.png)

![Shifted left]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_equivariance_shift_left.png)

![Shifted up + right]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_equivariance_shift_up.png)

The bounding boxes **move with** the cows.
:::


## Task → Required Property

| Task | Property | Why |
|------|----------|-----|
| **Classification** | Translation invariance | A cat is a cat anywhere |
| **Detection** | Translation equivariance | Box moves with the object |
| **Segmentation** | Translation equivariance | Pixel labels shift with input |


## The CNN Idea {.center}

::: {.incremental}
1. **Local connectivity** — neuron sees a small spatial region
2. **Parameter sharing** — same filter at every position
3. **Translation equivariance** — input shifts → output shifts
:::

::: {.fragment}
These encode our **prior knowledge** about images.
:::


## Local Connectivity

::: {#fig-cnn-cnn-spatial}
![Source: @johnson_eecs_2019]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cnn_spatial.jpg){width=25%}

A neuron only connects to a small spatial patch of the input.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Result: fewer parameters, preserved structure, position-agnostic detectors.
:::


## Inductive Bias

::: {.incremental}
- MLPs — minimal bias, very general, **data-hungry**
- CNNs — assume **locality + translation equivariance**
- Transformers — assume **long-range dependencies**
- GNNs — assume **graph structure**
:::

::: {.fragment}
Choosing an architecture = choosing which assumptions to bake in.
:::


# How CNNs Work


## CNN Architecture

::: {#fig-cnn-convnet}
![Source: @li_cs231n_2022]({{< meta params.images_path >}}convnet.jpeg){width=70%}

A sequence of layers transforms activations from input to predictions.
:::


## The Convolution Operation

$$
S(i, j) = (K * I)(i, j) = \sum_m \sum_n I(i + m, j + n)\, K(m, n)
$$

::: {.fragment}
- $I$ — input
- $K$ — kernel (smaller than $I$)
- $i, j$ — spatial position in the output
:::

::: {.fragment}
[CNN Explainer](https://poloclub.github.io/cnn-explainer/) — interactive demo.
:::


## Filter vs. Kernel

::: {.incremental}
- **Kernel** — 2-D ($H \times W$)
- **Filter** — 3-D ($C \times H \times W$); a stack of $C$ kernels
:::


## Convolution on RGB

::: {#fig-cnns-intro-example}
![Source: @prince_understanding_2023]({{< meta params.images_path >}}convolution_prince_rgb.png){width=70%}

A $3 \times 3 \times 3$ filter is multiplied element-wise with the input volume; sum → one output value.
:::


## Step by Step

::: {#fig-cnn-conv-step-by-step}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}conv_step_by_step.png){width=70%}

Slide the filter, compute $\sum (\text{patch} \odot \text{kernel}) + b$ at each position.
:::


## Multi-Channel Convolution

::: {#fig-cnn-conv-multi-channel}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}conv_rgb_channels.png){width=70%}

Each channel filtered separately; per-channel sums add up + bias → one scalar.
:::


## Multiple Filters → Output Volume

::: {#fig-cnn-conv-multi-filter}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}conv_multi_filter.png){width=70%}

Stack activation maps along the channel axis → output volume with $C_\text{out}$ channels.
:::

::: {.fragment}
In practice: 4-D tensors — $N \times C_\text{in} \times H \times W \to N \times C_\text{out} \times H' \times W'$.
:::


## Translation Equivariance

::: {#fig-cnn-translation-equivariance}

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/qoWAFBYOtoU start="50" width=1200 height=600 >}}

Same filter at every position → output shifts when input shifts.
:::

::: {.fragment}
For **invariance** (classification), add pooling or global average pooling.
:::


## Stride

::: {#fig-cnn-stride1}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}stride1_example.jpg){width=60%}

Stride 1 — filter moves one pixel at a time.
:::


## Stride 2 — Downsampling

::: {#fig-cnn-stride2}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}stride2_example.jpg){width=60%}

Stride 2 — moves two pixels at a time, halving the spatial size.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Strided convolution = **learned downsampling** (vs. fixed pooling).
:::


## Padding

::: {#fig-cnn-padding}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}padding_example_result.jpg){width=60%}

Zero-padding the border preserves spatial size — essential for segmentation.
:::


## Kernel Size

::: {#fig-cnn-kernel-size3x3}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}kernel_size_example_3x3.jpg){width=55%}

$3 \times 3$ kernel with padding — output size unchanged.
:::


## Larger Kernels

::: {#fig-cnn-kernel-size5x5}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}kernel_size_example_5x5.jpg){width=55%}

$5 \times 5$ kernel — wider receptive field, more parameters.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Modern design:** stack multiple $3 \times 3$ — fewer params, more nonlinearities.
:::


## Dilation

::: {#fig-cnn-dilation}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}dilation_example.jpg){width=60%}

Spread the kernel — larger receptive field, **same parameters**.
:::


## Why Dilation?

::: {.incremental}
- **Larger receptive field** without more layers
- **Same parameter count**
- **Multi-scale features** with varying dilation rates
:::

::: {.fragment}
Used in DeepLab (segmentation), WaveNet (audio), Dilated ResNets.
:::

::: {.fragment}
3×3 with dilation 2 → receptive field of 5×5, only 9 params (vs. 25).
:::


## Conv Animations

::: {.fragment}
![Source @dumoulin_guide_2016]({{< meta params.images_path >}}no_padding_no_strides.gif){width=20%}

3×3 kernel over 5×5 input, no padding, stride 1.
:::

[github.com/vdumoulin/conv_arithmetic](https://github.com/vdumoulin/conv_arithmetic)


## Output Size Formula

$$
o = \left\lfloor \frac{i + 2p - d \cdot (k-1) - 1}{s} + 1 \right\rfloor
$$

::: {.fragment}
- $i$ — input side length
- $k$ — kernel size
- $p$ — padding (per side)
- $s$ — stride
- $d$ — dilation
:::


## Quiz: Output Shape

$i = 32, \; k = 3, \; p = 1, \; s = 2, \; d = 1$. Find $o$.

::: {.fragment}
$$o = \left\lfloor \frac{32 + 2 - 1 \cdot 2 - 1}{2} + 1 \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{31}{2} + 1 \right\rfloor = 16$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Intuition:** stride 2 ≈ halves the spatial dim; padding preserves a bit.
:::


## Parameter Count

$$
\text{Weights} = k \times k \times C_\text{in} \times C_\text{out}
$$

::: {.fragment}
$$
\text{Total} = k \times k \times C_\text{in} \times C_\text{out} + C_\text{out}
$$
(plus one bias per output channel)
:::


## Quiz: Parameter Counting

Layer: $C_\text{in} = 3, \; C_\text{out} = 64, \; k = 5$, with bias.

::: {.fragment}
- **Weights**: $5 \times 5 \times 3 \times 64 = 4{,}800$
- **Biases**: $64$
- **Total**: $4{,}864$
:::

::: {.fragment}
A fully connected alternative ($32 \times 32 \times 3 \to 64$):
$$
196{,}608 \quad \text{parameters} \;\; (\text{40× more!})
$$
:::


## Stacking Convolutions

::: {#fig-cnn-conv-stacking}
![Source: @johnson_eecs_2019]({{< meta params.images_path >}}conv_stacking.jpg){width=60%}

Each layer operates on the previous layer's activation maps.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Non-linear activations between layers are **essential** — otherwise it collapses to a single linear conv.
:::


## Hierarchical Features

::: {#fig-cnn-conv-zeiler}
![Source: @Zeiler2014]({{< meta params.images_path >}}zeiler_learned_filters.png){width=55%}

Filters: edges → textures → parts → objects (deeper layers respond to more complex patterns).
:::


## Receptive Field — One Layer

::: {#fig-cnn-receptive-field-1}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}receptive_field1.jpg){width=60%}

Single layer with a 5×5 kernel.
:::


## Receptive Field — Two Layers

::: {#fig-cnn-receptive-field-4}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}receptive_field4.jpg){width=70%}

Two stacked 5×5 convolutions → **9×9** receptive field.
:::


## Receptive Field Formula

$$
r_0 = \sum_{l=1}^L \left( (k_l - 1) \prod_{i=1}^{l-1} s_i \right) + 1
$$

::: {.fragment}
Stacking small kernels grows the field efficiently.
:::


## Quiz: Receptive Field

- Layer 1: kernel=3, stride=1
- Layer 2: kernel=3, stride=2
- Layer 3: kernel=5, stride=1

::: {.fragment}
$r_0 = (3-1)\cdot 1 + (3-1)\cdot 1 + (5-1)\cdot(1 \cdot 2) + 1$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$r_0 = 2 + 2 + 8 + 1 = \mathbf{13}$ → **13 × 13** receptive field.
:::


## Pooling

::: {#fig-cnn-downsampling-pooling}
![Source: @prince_understanding_2023]({{< meta params.images_path >}}downsampling_with_pooling.jpg){width=70%}

(a) Sub-sampling, (b) Max pooling, (c) Average pooling.
:::


## 1×1 Convolutions

::: {#fig-cnn-1x1-conv}
![Source: @prince_understanding_2023]({{< meta params.images_path >}}1x1_conv_example.jpg){width=60%}

Change number of channels with few parameters: $C \times H \times W \to C_2 \times H \times W$ uses only $C_2 \times (C + 1)$ params.
:::


## Global Average Pooling

::: {#fig-cnn-global-avg-pooling}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}global_average_pooling.jpg){width=60%}

Average each map → $(C \times H \times W) \to (C \times 1 \times 1)$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Provides translation **invariance** — and replaces fully-connected heads.
:::


# Summary {.center}


## Key Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- MLPs flatten images → lose structure, explode in size
- CNNs encode **locality + parameter sharing + translation equivariance** as inductive biases
- Conv hyperparameters: kernel, stride, padding, dilation — control receptive field & output size
- Stacked convs grow receptive fields and learn **hierarchical features**
- Pooling, 1×1 conv, global avg pool — workhorse layers around convolutions
:::
